title: How Crime Scene Photography Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore crime scene photography: its origins with Alphonse Bertillon, who also devised mug shots and an anthropometric measurement system later undermined by the 1903-era Leavenworth William West case; the three classes of forensic photos (overview, mid-range, close-up); scale rulers and duplicate shots; photolog and honesty requirements; standard operating procedure such as depth of field and sharpness; chain of custody and image security; the photography kit; video and infrared use; blood spatter projection; and the news photographer Weegee (Arthur Fellig) and his photo "Their First Murder." The episode closes with a listener birthday shout-out.
topics: Manhattan District Attorney crime scene unit

segments.title: Opening banter and camera ad lead-in
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, a camera sponsor tagline, and a joke about a camera-themed intro that leads into the crime scene photography topic.

segments.title: Alphonse Bertillon, mug shots, and the Bertillon measurement system
segments.summary: Bertillon, a 19th-century French photographer, is credited with forensic crime scene photography and with mug shots. He was also tied to eugenics and devised eleven body measurements. A Leavenworth clerk matched a new prisoner, William West, to an existing William West with identical measurements, undermining the system.

segments.title: Origins of systematic crime scene photography
segments.summary: Bertillon was the first to apply method to crime scene photography, using multiple angles, close-ups, and whole-scene surveys. Earlier crime photos were often sensational newspaper images. Evidence is transitory, so photographers must document the scene before it is disturbed.

segments.title: Manhattan DA's crime scene unit and the three photo classifications
segments.summary: The Manhattan District Attorney's Office has its own photography unit dispatched independently of police. Forensic photos fall into overview, mid-range, and close-up categories, covering building exteriors, entrances, crowds, all rooms, and the murder weapon in context.
topics: Manhattan District Attorney crime scene unit

segments.title: Scale references, photolog, and standard procedure
segments.summary: Close-ups are taken with a scale ruler and again without it so the defense cannot claim it hid evidence. Photologs record details manually in older days. Standard procedure requires sharp focus, maximum depth of field, no sensationalism, and no obstruction of evidence.

segments.title: Chain of custody and image security
segments.summary: Hosts discuss chain of custody for cameras and digital files, preserving originals, logging any manipulation, and storing backups with image security software. Honesty and no emotional bias are emphasized.

segments.title: Forensic photo kit, video, infrared, and blood spatter
segments.summary: The kit includes cameras, wide, mid, and zoom lenses, filters, and a light meter with a gray card. Color is typical, with black and white sometimes used for latent prints. Video is now common and often shot before stills. Infrared film helps with dark scenes. Blood spatter can be projected life-size later.

segments.title: Weegee and Their First Murder
segments.summary: Weegee (Arthur Fellig), a 1920s to 1950s photojournalist, lived near a Manhattan police station, monitored a police scanner, and had informants. He photographed crowds' emotional reactions, including the photo Their First Murder from Williamsburg, and his work was later shown in galleries. A 2001 Los Angeles find of old forensic photos, including possibly Black Dahlia material, is mentioned.

segments.title: Birthday shout-out for Graham Baker
segments.summary: A listener requests a birthday shout-out for her boyfriend Graham Baker. The hosts wish him well and invite listeners to send other mail.
